subtopic: RAISING OF PRIME LENDING RATE BY CHARTERED BANKS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
RAISING OF PRIME LENDING RATE BY CHARTERED BANKS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask the house to agree to a motion which I shall read in a moment. Perhaps I might read Standing Order 43, which is as follows:
A motion may, in case of urgent and pressing necessity previously explained by the mover, be made by unanimous consent of the house without notice having been given under Standing Order 42.
The Standing Order provides the opportunity for a short explanation. May I do so briefly, Mr. Speaker?
It is obvious to all that interest rates have been rising continuously, creating an unjust and inequitable burden for the Canadian public, culminating Thursday in a decision by the Canadian chartered banks to charge 7.5 per cent as their prime lending rate. If this trend is permitted to continue housing and public policy at the federal, provincial and municipal levels may be frustrated.
This is the result of the amendments to the Bank Act made in 1967, which removed the interest level ceiling that banks could charge for loans, and which also gave the chartered banks more flexibility to take deposits and lend money. The possibility of this situation arising was recognized by the committee at
that time, and in the committee report they said as follows:
Your committee recognizes-

speechtext: Order, please. My interpretation of Standing Order 43 is that the explanation which the hon. member may give to the house at this time should be brief and succinct. I think we will get ourselves into serious difficulties if every day, under the guise of Standing Order 43, hon. members were to make long speeches and to suggest that there might be unanimous consent and agreement of the house to discuss a grievance of some kind. I believe that for the good and orderly consideration of the house business the statement being made by the hon. member at the present time should be brief.

subtopic: RAISING OF PRIME LENDING RATE BY CHARTERED BANKS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

That the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs be authorized to meet forthwith and proceed as quickly as possible to investigate, analyse, and hear evidence on the Bank Act. the Bank of Canada Act and the Quebec Savings Bank Act.

subtopic: UNCOLLECTIBLE STUDENT LOANS
UNCOLLECTIBLE STUDENT LOANS
speechtext: What is the total amount that has been written off as uncollectable under the Canada Student Loans Plan from its inception to December 31, 1968?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: UNCOLLECTIBLE STUDENT LOANS
speechtext:
Under Section 8 of the Canada Student Loans Act, a borrower's obligation is extinguished in the event of his death whereupon it becomes payable by the government on the borrower's behalf. Since the inception of the Plan to December 31, 1968, $137,000 was paid under Section 8. This amount is not recoverable from the estates of deceased borrowers.

Under Section 9 of the Canada Student Loans Act, the government is required to reimburse a bank against loss incurred in connection with loans in default. Once a claim is paid by the government to a bank under this guarantee, the borrower's obligation is then owed to the Crown, but continues to exist. Collection action is continued to retire the debt then owing to the Crown, including certain costs chargeable to the borrower. Since the inception of the Plan to December 31, 1968, $507,090 were paid in respect of defaulted loans. This amount remains recoverable from the borrowers, and none of it has been written off. An additional $22,000 was paid during the same period for costs not recoverable from borrowers.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF MOTOR VEHICLE SAFETY STANDARDS
CANCELLATION OF MOTOR VEHICLE SAFETY STANDARDS
speechtext: Were motor vehicle safety standards formerly issued by the Canadian Government Specifications Board cancelled for: height and extension of bumpers, rear-window vision aid, ash trays and lighters, head-rests for front seas, roll bars, outside ornamentation, accessories and profusions, rear luggage compartment carrier and, if so, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: CANCELLATION OF MOTOR VEHICLE SAFETY STANDARDS
speechtext: In so far as the Department of Defence Production is concerned: Yes. Due to the Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement, the Canadian automotive industry became committed to adjusting their total production to conform to U.S. mandatory standards and it was not desirable to continue the Canadian Government Specifications Board motor vehicle standards for features that could not then be made available without undue delay and expense. Since that time the cancelled standard for Head Rests for front seats has been replaced by an improved standard. The development of replacement Canadian Government Specification Board standards for height and extension of bumpers, rear-window vision aids, ash trays and lighters, roll bars, outside ornamentation, accessories and protrusions and rear luggage compartment barrier is underway in line with parallel action in the United States.

speechtext:
1.	What were the subsidies, per ton, paid by the federal government during the 1966-67 crop year for the transportation (a) by ship (b) by rail, of feed grains, from the Lakehead to the various ports on the St. Lawrence?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: TRANSPORTATION SUBSIDIES ON FEED GRAIN
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned: 1. The average subsidy per ton paid by the federal government on shipments of feed grains during the crop year 1966-67 to destinations in the Province of Ontario was $5.28, to destinations in the Province of Quebec was $7.68, and to destinations in the Atlantic Provinces was $13.17. The rates of freight assistance on feed grains under the Feed Grain Assistance Regulations of the Livestock Feed Assistance Act are the same whether the grain has been transported by rail or by ship.
2.	Since the rate of assistance does not differ between water and rail movement, data on freight assistance paid on each separately are not available. During the crop year 1966-67, 2,472,524 tons of feed grains were shipped into Eastern Canada under the program, at a total cost of $18,394,712.
3.	No difference exists in rates of assistance applicable to rail and ship movement.
4.	The Board of Grain Commissioners is responsible for the general supervision of storage and movement of grain through the Eastern Elevators that are licensed under the Canada Grain Act. The Board's principal responsibility relates to the licensing of the elevators, the inspection and weighing of the grain, the rates permitted to be charged for storing and handling grain at the licensed elevators, the registration of documents covering the grain, and the reporting of details of stock and handlings. Official sampling and inspection service is available on request at eastern elevators.
Under the Inland Water Freight Rates Act the Board of Grain Commissioners has authority to set maximum rates that apply on Canadian lake grain cargoes.
The Board of Grain Commissioners is not involved in the actual merchandising of grain.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORDERS
subsubtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND CANADIAN FORCES, DEFENCE SERVICES, R.C.M.P. AND PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION PROVISIONS- REPORT STAGE
speechtext:
That Bill C-178, to amend the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pension Continuation Act and the Public Service Superannuation Act, be amended by deleting therefrom clauses 19, 34 and 48.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we are now at the report stage of Bill C-178 which seeks to amend a number of statutes under which pensions are provided for various categories of employees of the federal government.
As I indicated when we were at second reading of this bill, the bill for the most part is good legislation. Most of the changes are improvements that will be for the benefit of persons covered by the various statutes. I also made it clear that there was a serious deficiency in the bill because it includes no provision for increasing the pensions of civil servants already retired and it also makes no provision for escalating after retirement the pensions of persons covered under the act.
March 24, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act
Do you think- those dollars come out of a trust account, a bank account, or the Bank of Canada? No. They came off the figures on the book, but the dollars themselves come out of current revenues, the current funds of the government of Canada which come out of current production.
I contend that to the extent that we try to play up, dress up and fool around with these funds we are simply fooling the people of Canada. I quite agree that when I ask for higher pensions for those who are now retired, and when I ask for a provision for those now working that their pensions shall be escalated after their retirement, I am not relying on a fund. I am not arguing that this should be done because there are so many dollars in the fund because I know there is nothing there. But what I am doing is calling for a deliberate decision. I am calling for our society to say that just as people who are working deserve decent rates of wages and salaries, so people who are retired are entitled to a pension that will enable them to live in the circumstances that obtain during their years of retirement.
When- I ask that the pensions of those now retired be increased it is because I think we owe it to them as a matter of good faith, we owe it in recognition of what they have done in the past, we owe it because some of us believe that retired people have just as much right to keep up with rising standards as those who are working, and we believe that pensions should escalate in the same manner as wages and salaries escalate. But, Mr. Speaker, let us get to the reality of the situation, and let us not try to fool ourselves by a fund of this kind.
We do the same kind of thing with regard to old age security. We say to our people that they get their old age security payments out of a fund, and that so much money is put into a fund. Again it is an account, and there are taxes for it, 4 per cent, 3 per cent and 3 per cent. But if I were to get up in the House of Commons, as I have been tempted to do in the last few days, and point out that there is a credit balance in the old age security fund of $642 million, and since that money has been collected for old age security purposes it ought to be paid out in old age pensions, I would be told that the money is not in a special fund; it is just a bookkeeping proposition.
The reason that the people of Canada get old age security payments is that the government of Canada, the people of Canada and the economy of the nation are all behind the


guarantee to pay these pensions. That is what pensions payments are. They are guarantees that out of current production these payments will be made. I contend that what is going on here, this attempt to fiddle around with the accounting procedures, is a case of getting away from the realities of the pension situation. Indeed, it is a case of trying to fool our retired civil servants, just as we try to fool the people on old age security generally by telling them there is a fund when no fund exists at all.
I know that there are people on the other side of the house, even people in the cabinet, who share this view that the business of funding government pensions is unreal. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), when he was minister of finance, admitted to me at one time when we were d.scussing the old age security question that the fund itself was only so many figures in a book, that it might as well be done away with, and that we might as well recognize the fact that we are agreeing, as a society, what pensions we will pay to our retired people out of current production. That is what the Public Service Superannuation act is all about. It is an act under which in good faith the government of Canada says to its employees, "If you work for us for 10, 20, 30 or 35 years, and if you will take less than the full amount of your pay we will undertake in the name of Canada, in the name of our people, in the name of the resources we have, that after your retirement you will have a decent standard of living."
In the past we thought we were giving effect to that promise by providing a certain formula related to salaries and wages during a certain period of time. It was a ten year period, then five years, and now it is six years. But times have changed. We are in the age of explosions. Things are moving a lot faster than they used to, and people are living a lot longer. The rates of pensions applicable at age 60 or 65 are not good enough at 75, 80 or 85. Nowadays a good many people are living in retirement for periods of 15 years, 20 years or 25 years. In such a long period of time our economy changes. It changes so much that it is not good enough to have a formula that ties pensions to a rate fixed at the time of retirement. If we go along with this type of legislation, the kind of provision in these three clauses I am speaking against, tied to a particular fund or particular account, and say, "You cannot get more no matter how high a rate of interest we pay on the fund," we are just not keeping faith with
March 24, 1969	COMMONS
the people to whom we have said, "Work tor us and we will see to it that you will have a decent retirement."
That is why I think that these three clauses, 19, 34 and 48, should not be passed. Instead of fooling the people this way with these funds and this kind of accounting, we should put this thing on a realistic basis. We should say to our people, "There is no fund. No dollars have been set aside."
Today, just to refresh myself and to make sure of what I am saying, I picked up a copy of the public accounts for last year. I found that last year the amount of money that public service employees had deducted from their pay was greater than the amount that was paid out in the same year in pensions. There are some things to add on both sides. The payments out also included transfers to other funds and things of that sort. Payments in included government contributions, matching contributions, transfers from other pensions, funds and so on. But the fact is that in the total the government does not pay in any year 100 per cent of its wage bill, even when you add the pensions to the salaries being paid. This is the reality.
I want to convert this reality into a just system, even if I have to call for a just society. I want to convert this into a society where we say to the people who work for the federal government, "If you work for us in your working years we will see to it that in retirement you will have a pension that will enable you to live in those years of retirement in a manner commensurate with the standard of living in that period of time."
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I want this, and I am sure the house knows it now, not just for our retired civil servants and those who come under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, and so on, but for those who work for Canadian National Railways, Canadian Pacific Railway and all our people. I want it for the old age security pensioner as well, that is, the provision for pensions in the period of retirement to escalate not just according to the cost of living but according to rising wages and salaries, in other words, according to the increase in productivity and the increase in the affluence of our society.
But we will not get it with this kind of dead-hand bookkeeping. We will not get it with this kind of fooling around with the books that seems to add interest in which
DEBATES	7011
Statute Law Amendment Act people think they have some rights because it is interest on their money. Then the government turns around and says that despite the additional interest these people should not look for any more money because it is going to pay less by way of special payments year by year. In the end the total will be precisely the same, and there is nothing in it for our retired people.
This is not the kind of legislation that we should be passing. I say again, as I said at the start and on second reading, that most of Bill C-178 is good. It provides improvements that will be for the benefit of employees of the federal government-those now working, at any rate. It does not provide anything for those already retired. It does not provide anything for those now working, because at the time of retirement they will be in the same box as those already retired.
To me this is an extremely important issue in our society and our economy, namely, what we do for our older people. We have not finished the job because we have an old age security pension, a guaranteed income supplement, a Public Service Superannuation Act and a whole host of pension schemes both public and private. We will not, in my view, finish the job until we have these pension schemes on a basis where after retirement people are able to keep up with the standard of living that improves during that period of time. Pensions have to escalate, not just according to the cost of living but according to increased productivity. This will not happen so long as you have the dead-hand kind of bookkeeping proposed in these three clauses. That is why I think the house should reject these three clauses and let the rest of the bill pass without them.
The only other comment I wish to make is that I hope this is the last time the government will bring before us a bill to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act and the acts related thereto without having in it something to provide for increased pensions for those already retired, and something to provide that those who are now working will when they retire be awarded pensions that will escalate during their period of retirement in keeping with increased wages and salaries, in keeping with the increased productivity and affluence of our society.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the house and apologize to the minister and hon. members for not being here when the debate started, but an urgent personal matter had taken me out of
March 24, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act the house just after two o'clock. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has used the term "dead-hand bookkeeping". He says this is at the source of the problem with the superannuation fund for public civil servants and the scale of their pensions. I do not think it is dead-hand bookkeeping that is causing the problem; I think it is a dead-hand principle behind the handling of the pension fund. It is not in the matter of bookkeeping; that is mere mechanics.
Over the years we have seen more and more of Canada's population come into the public service of this country. We have seen more and more people enter the armed services and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. If those people were out in what one could call non-public service, working for a corporation or individuals, they would have funded pension plans. The moneys available from the pension fund would be invested in economic productivity, in productive investment-in equities, preferred shares, any type of corporate financing plus, of course, government bonds in order to get the appropriate mix. There would also be money available for housing. Instead of that, all the money goes into the consolidated revenue fund and merely remains there for general government purposes. There is an appropriation, I suppose, to the superannuation fund but the money is not invested as such; it merely remains as a charge on the consolidated revenue fund.
That is why the hon. member is able to say there is this sort of dead-hand bookkeeping, because all it is is bookkeeping. I put it to the government that it would be far better if it introduced into the Public Service Superannuation Act orthodox funding principles whereby the money taken from people working in Canada, plus the contribution of the employer, would be invested in an appropriate plan of securities, provincial and federal, corporate equities and other debt instruments,
I suggest to the government this would eliminate the need for the theory put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that pension funds should be tied into some sort of formula that goes along with productivity. The hon. member's party would like it tied to the cost of living index. This is self-defeating. Tying pensions to the cost of living index on this basis is merely self-defeating; it generates more inflation and the net result is that every year we get up over the 2 per cent and add more to pensions. I suggest that is merely generating more inflationary pressure.


On the other hand, I would put forward the suggestion, and I think it is sound economics, that government pension plans, not only that of the federal but those of the provincial governments, should be invested in the productivity of Canada. Thereby these pension funds would reflect the increase in the value of equities, debt instruments and increasing profits due to increases in productivity. This is precisely what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been asking for. Then pensions could be adjusted if need be. In other words, our pensioners would have part of the action.
This is what we now get from mortgage companies who want "a piece of the action" because they want to share in the increase in productivity, in the increase in value. Why should our pensioners not have the same advantage? They have made their pension fund contributions, which is a forced method of saving, the employer has matched them, and the money should then be put to work. Why should not the employee, the pensioner, get the benefit of the profits that have been earned through the pension fund? I am sure that in this way we would have a much greater source of funds and the government would have a much better pension scheme. The government should set an example in this regard. We would do away with calls for Canada development corporations and all sorts of dubious proposals because we would have a very large pension fund administered properly by trustees on behalf of employees who have a real interest in the fund. At the present time they have no say with regard to the fund. Whether or not they shall be paid an increase is entirely up to the government.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I agree with my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), in the same way as I agreed with my former colleague from Carleton, the Hon. Richard Bell, who times without number advanced the proposal that something must be done to reduce the disparity between the level of pensions of former public servants and that of those who are now entering their pension life. The gap in pension levels is far too wide, as there are great disparities in salary levels. One has only to go through the whole scale of salaries in the public service as against those in industry to see that there are horrible gaps and disparities. But the most glaring one is the result of a comparison between a public servant who retired 10 or 12 years ago and one who retires now.

If I recall correctly, the last time any change was made was in 1958 or 1959 when the then minister of finance upgraded minimum pensions of those who had retired prior to 1953. The formula was complicated but the measure was only a palliative and did not go far enough. In 1958 and 1959, however, there were other problems of financing, and this was something that came out of the consolidated revenue fund. Hon. members must remember that a pension that is once effected must remain that way; it can never be downgraded.

Mr. Speaker, in introducing this amendment the mover said that he thought he was bringing the argument one step further toward reality. I regret I cannot subscribe to this point of view after listening to the debate. As nearly as I can understand it, the mover of the amendment believes that this fund is a publicly supported one and he does not distinguish it from the old age security fund or the type of fund which we set up for the Canada Pension Plan.
The second speaker took a totally different point of view. He suggested a totally funded approach in line with conventional methods and with all the requirements of the actuaries. He even went as far as to say that a similar approach should be taken with municipal and provincial funds and that out of the earnings of a fully developed type of plan additional pensions could be paid.
I think it is most unfortunate that this debate has taken place because I believe it is
March 24, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act
totally beside the point. As far as I can determine the purpose of the amendment is to strike out the provisions by which the government is attempting to bring the interest rates that are to be paid, in line with current interest rates. At the same time the government is calling attention to the fact that, as the result of the revisions of pay that have taken place, around $200 million a year in respect of arrears to compensate for these pay adjustments is being paid in the current fiscal year. If one were to increase the fund's interest yield by something like 3 per cent, no more than $100 million would be gained by way of additional interest. In my opinion the government is trying to do certain things to introduce a measure of reality into what has become a most unfortunate discussion.
I have supported the principle of increasing the pensions of superannuated civil servants as consistently and as forcibly as any member in the period that I have been in this house. But I do take violent exception to a debate which leads to a grave misconception on the part of pensioners. A debate took place in the house on second reading on March 14. Subsequent to that debate I have received a substantial volume of mail because I took part in it and I said I was in favour of increasing pensions, as did a number of other hon. members. The kind of letters we are getting will increase in frequency as a result of this debate. Many old age pensioners, after listening to what I consider to be arguments that are completely beside the point, have come to the conclusion that the government has stolen the fund and that there is something grossly irregular about it. They suspect irregular management and they think the Auditor General should be called in. They are giving a totally erroneous interpretation to what has taken place.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I said before and I repeat that the case for the adjustment of pensions is a moral case. I believe the government of Canada should set an example in respect of those who have worked for it and are now in retirement, and do the things we would like other good employers to do. But I have to adopt some consistency about this approach. A private employer who sets up a pension plan in this country is required by law in most of the provinces, certainly in the larger ones-in some provinces the jurisdiction is not as tight as it should be, nor is the supervision as effective as it should be-to make certain provisions to guarantee the solvency of the

fund. He must protect as far as possible those who have claims on it.
In my opinion the government, in its capacity as employer, should set a model, and I expect that role to apply not only in connection with pensions but in connection with general levels of remuneration, the standards applied to collective bargaining and a broad range of legislative policy. What we do in respect of those who work for us should be a model upon the basis of which we are able to say to other employers in Canada: Please follow this example.

speechtext:
I deplore this debate. I
deplore the very fact it has had to take place, because I know I shall get another wave of letters. I shall put one or two of them on record in Hansard if I may-those portions which are printable; some parts of them may not be written in parliamentary language and, if so, I might be called to account. I quote from a letter dated March 18 which I received signed by E. P. Gray:
Lloyd Francis:
On an Open Line show over CKOY a lady civil servant superannuate read tor the benefit of listeners correspondence between the lady and you concerning the cold-blooded manner in which the Liberal government is handling the requests for an increase in their pensions from their own money.
And, Mr. Speaker, "their own" is underlined.
I knew you were a revolting, thieving, shifty-bastard, Francis, and am pleased that now a great many more are aware of your sickening character.
After that, Mr. Speaker, it really gets abusive.
That is not the only letter to which I shall refer, Mr. Speaker. Another one, dated March 16, said: "This money belongs to us superannuates; what has the government done with it?" The kind of thing which is being said is somehow being spread from sources which should know better. Someone is deliberately giving misinformation to a broad range of retired superannuates concerning the management of the fund.
I fail to see what anyone could gain by prolonging a debate of this nature. I fail to see what the mover of the motion hopes to gain by striking out this provision to bring interest rates up to current standards of interest rates. We are saying to the employers of this country: this is what we want you to do as employers, but it is totally different for us because we have a public fund and we can
March 24, 1969	COMMONS
do things as we wish; it does not matter whether or not we pay the current interest rate, though you, as private employers, must do all these things. For this reason I cannot support the amendment. I do not see what useful purpose is being served.
I personally believe that the government has a moral obligation, one to which I hope it will respond at the earliest possible date, to raise the pensions of its retired employees. This argument is lost if one tries to become an amateur actuary, if one tries to say: this year the fund paid out so much and took in so much. No person can pass judgment on the state of such a fund by looking at income and expenditure in a one-year period or a two-year period or a three-year period. The fund can only be appraised by those who know the extent of the claims made upon it, or likely to be made upon it, and of the resources available to meet them. We should not try to set ourselves up as experts of that kind, because we are not. We are not actuaries. We are not competent to pass judgment on the extent of the solvency of the fund. In my opinion it serves no useful purpose for us to say: this is what a private employer must do, but the government can violate all the rules and everything is O.K. This, I cannot accept, and for this reason I shall vote against the amendment.

I spoke on the second reading stage of this bill, Mr. Speaker. Now we are on the report stage and I wish to add a few words.
I do not think the situation in which we find ourselves is very fortunate. Today, while we are talking about superannuation, we are still working on old principles. The contents of this bill are good, as was mentioned a few minutes ago, for civil servants who are still working, but they mean nothing to those who have retired and little to those who will retire in the future because they will ultimately be in the same position as public servants whc retired some years ago.
I must differ from my hon. friend, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), in at least one respect. He says the obligation we have to retired public servants is a moral one. In my opinion it is not a moral one; it is a matter of justice and equity. It is up to the government to decide that what was done in the past was not necessarily best.
I can speak clearly and openly on this issue. I was chairman of the committee which recommended amendments to the superannuation legislation and considered the plight of retired public servants. We thoroughly considered the questions of funding, the payment of higher interest credits to the fund, and so on. I am not an accountant nor an economist and perhaps this is why I am more interested in the welfare and well-being of the people who are actually involved in this question today.
I am still bothered by the thought that far too many former civil servants have no way of getting an income that is in any way reasonable except through an increase in their pensions. In my opinion the means employed to bring this about are secondary. I am not
7016	COMMONS
Statute Law Amendment Act interested in whether this fund is being operated in a manner similar to that in which other funds are legally operating at the present time. I am interested, rather, in what the government intends to do to make it possible for those who have retired on pensions now shown to be inadequate to receive suitable increases. We have been talking about a guaranteed income in the future to provide people with enough to live on properly. Surely if we start by doing something for our retired public servants we will at least have closed the gap to some extent and we will not have to look after these people under some other scheme.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Surely this fund should be credited with a rate of interest that is more up to date. The old rate of 4 per cent is certainly an antique. It reminds that other money is being lent at a low rate of interest to the provinces through the Canada Pension Plan. Perhaps this money should also have been invested in some other way. There is no reason why money which will later be credited to pensions for the people of Canada should receive a lower rate of interest than the current rate simply because it is used to finance the municipalities and provinces of this country. However, that is another matter.
I just wanted to say that I have nothing particularly against the provisions of this bill because I do not think anyone will be harmed. I should have liked to see some provision made for higher interest rates for funds that are used for a definite purpose at the present time. In the same way that many funds of corporations are now making provision for raising the pensions of their retired employees, in a very few years we shall have to change the method we use to provide for pensions of public servants. I am sure this will be done fairly soon when some of the people who have been blocking progress in this regard have retired.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few brief comments on this bill. There is no doubt whatever that many retired members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, retired civil servants and former members of our armed forces are among the main victims of inflation. Many of these people live in my constituency and elsewhere in British Columbia. We are supposed to enjoy a fairly good measure of affluence in the province of British Columbia, yet 25 per cent of the people of that prosperous province

DEBATES	March 24. 1969
live on less than $3,000 a year. These include famihes. Among the people living under difficult circumstances are many in the category to which this amendment is addressed.
Together with other members of the house I support increases for the superannuates in the categories referred to. However, apart from the consideration of amendments of this kind, I think provision should be made for an escalation device as a hedge against the future erosion of superannuates' purchasing power. Surely we should be working toward achieving price stability in this country for all people, superannuates and others.
At the same time, we should have special regard for former employees of the public service. We should be the first in this country to make sure that they are indemnified in terms of their purchasing power and not merely in terms of the face value of the dollar bills they receive by way of pension. When former members of the R.C.M.P. and the public service retire, surely they have earned the right to live with dignity.
I have in my hand a copy of a letter I received from a former R.C.M.P. sergeant who is living in my constituency of Burnaby-Seymour. He says in part:
We have made a canvas among a good number of our senior members who served full time in the service of their country and who are receiving pensions that hardly look after their rent. Some of them are in destitute circumstances. The last increase in R.C.M.P. pensions was in 1959. There are a number of us who are gainfully employed and who do not have to fully depend on a pension (thank God). I had 24 years of service, being pensioned in 1956 as a sergeant. My pension is approximately $2,700 per annum. My salary when pensioned was $4,980 per annum, whereas a sergeant today receives $9,074 and if leaving on pension at 24 years under Part Three of the R.C.M.P. Act, would receive approximately $425 per month in comparison to my pension of approximately $225, so you can see that in 12 years the pension has been almost doubled, and this has been brought on by the cost of living index rising every year with the resultant raises in salaries. The pensioners' income should rise along with the raises in pay and cost of living index, but they remain stagnant.
I agree with what this retired R.C.M.P. sergeant has to say. We have to set an example in this country by proving that those who establish a career with the government, whether they be members of the R.C.M.P., civil servants or members of the armed forces, enjoy fair treatment on the part of the federal government and are given the right to live with dignity. We owe it to these people to make sure that they are able to enjoy a reasonable degree of security in today's inflationary environment. We have to think not
March 24, 1969

only in terms of helping those who are former members of the R.C.M.P. and the civil service but also those who have fought the good fight in the past, have served loyally and faithfully and today are among the chief victims of inflation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words) to say about the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act. I
March 24, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act should like to draw the attention of the house to some things which have been happening in respect of the Canadian forces. This matter has been raised on a number of occasions by members on this side of the house and I know that a great number of members on the government side have also become aware of it. The Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the interpretation thereof is, frankly, being used as a blackjack to keep men in the armed services. It is also being used to exercise discriminatory ways of handling men who decide they wish to withdraw from the services for different reasons. I am aware of many cases concerning particularly men in the non-officer category. What happens sometimes is that the serviceman applies to get out of the service because he does not like it. Frankly, this may still be the result of unification. They have very much in mind the words of the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) when he was minister of national defence, that no man would be penalized as a result of his written request to get out.
I say that never was anything so false said or words so turned around, because scores and scores of cases have now come to my attention, and I know my colleagues have many other cases, in respect of which the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act has been used deliberately to keep men within the services. We know now that the morale among the members of the armed services has admittedly been bad and is worse. There are great gaps at the various levels within the services.
I have a particular case which I drew to the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) who is looking into it. There are cases involving two men who worked alongside one another. One man states that he wants to get out; he does not want to re-engage. He is a long-service man who has had 22 years and 132 days' service. He was subjected to a penalty of 10 per cent. He had to pay back a portion of his re-enlistment bonus of $600. Since he left the service he met his former pal who had worked at the same place. This man had refused a transfer to another base. He was near the end of his engagement. It was decided to release him under some other provision. He was not penalized the 10 per cent nor did he have to repay his enlistment bonus or a portion thereof. Why the different treatment? There are numerous cases of this kind.
I have spoken to the Minister of National Defence, and all the while he exhibits the

best of good will in cases of this kind and I know he is embarrassed by the situation. I wish to point out clearly to his senior military advisers that what they have been doing in these cases represents a breach of faith with the men and officers of the armed services as a result of unification. There have been far too many complaints and, shall we say, far too many instances of discrimination. Sometimes a man commits a minor offence which is just short of serious trouble and he is discharged for the good of the service. Often the person involved does not want to re-engage; he wants out. This man is simply told that he is being discharged. These men are happy to get out in any event regardless of the nature of the discharge.
It seems also that there have been some very friendly arrangements in respect of some discharges concerning whether or not the re-enlistment bonus should be returned. It is like the case of the old golden bowler. There was dishonesty with regard to some men who applied for this retirement bonus. Yet everything was done on an alleged up and up basis.
That is all I intend to say on this matter, but I wish it clearly understood that I know of scores and scores of cases of discrimination in discharges. The minister himself cannot look into all of these individual cases, but I suggest he should really step down hard on a number of types of cases. I do not know how he will manage this-I am not in the armed services-but this situation must be remedied. In many cases those who are affected are corporals and sergeants, the men who have considerable service. These are the persons who have been the experienced backbone of the services and have from 10 to 20 years service. Sometimes these people find that a person serving with them is given preferential treatment. If anything will hurt morale in the services this is it.
I say with all seriousness that I have a great admiration for the Canadian Armed Forces and a great love for them. What has been done is a matter of record. I grieve for these people. Finally, on the basis of an ex gratia payment an error is admitted and things are corrected. This is all I have to say on this occasion but I hope we will see some amelioration in the handling of superannuation.

Mr. Speaker, I did not take part in the debate on second reading and my remarks
March 24, 1989	COMMONS
now will be short but I hope they will be to the point. I am concerned about this legislation in so far as it affects retired public servants, retired members of the R.C.M..P and retired members of the armed forces, but I particularly wish to deal with the question of the superannuated public servants.
I cannot forget the fact that in reply to questions placed on the order paper by my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre last December, information was received to the effect that 7,201 public servants were receiving pensions of less than $60 a month. That means that one-fifth of all the retired public servants are being asked to exist on less than $60 a month. In addition, some 8,000 widows of retired public servants receive less than $60 a month. That means that half of the widows of deceased public servants receive less than $60 a month.
We are dealing here with human beings and not just figures in a book. With today's prices no one can live on $60 a month. These people are not retired, they are rejected, they are neglected, they are thrown on the scrap heap, they are despised by the government that deals with them.
In May, 1967, a joint committee of the House and Senate made a unanimous recommendation that the pensions of these three groups of people should be raised. Whenever the question has been raised in the house since that time we have been given the runaround. We have been told that the matter is under consideration. We have been told it is being looked at. We have been told to wait until this report or that finding is brought in. And all the time these people are expected to exist on $60 a month; all the time the cost of living has been escalating. Last year alone it went up by 4 per cent.
In my view this is a gross betrayal of people who have given the best years of their service to their country. I do not think this betrayal should be obscured by the kind of talk we have had this afternoon. These are not just bookkeeping entries. The cost of living has gone up and these pensions should contain an escalator clause.
It is all very well for members on the government side to applaud these retired public servants. I noted one member from my own province whose heart fairly dripped blood and whose eyes were washed with tears at the plight of our retired public servants. Yet he got up and voted for this legislation under which the government will pay a higher rate of interest on superannuation fund accounts,
DEBATES	7019
Statute Law Amendment Act but none of this extra money is to be used to pay higher pensions. What kind of honesty and integrity can people expect with that sort of thing?
This legislation provides for the payment by the government of higher rates of interest on superannuation funds for retired public servants, retired members of the R.C.M.P. and of the armed forces, but it also provides that no extra money will be paid in pensions. This is simply showing contempt for the people in these three categories who have worked for this country. I feel it is a great tragedy that the amendment moved by my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre has been defeated.
Once again we shall have letters flowing on to our desks from people who desperately watch the cost of living rise and try to live on pensions of $60 a month or less. A great many of these pensions are only $20 a month. This is an impossible injustice. I feel sure the people of this country will not remain quiescent when they realize what the government has done today. Its action is definitely giving the no to the unanimous recommendation two years ago of the Senate and House of Commons joint committee. It is giving a definite no to the people who had hoped that recognition would be given to the principle that retirement allowances should keep up with the cost of living. These people have asked for bread; they have been given the stone of neglect and complete rejection.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say before we give third reading to this bill. First, may I say that all the pleas by government members that they are just as sympathetic to the cause of retired civil servants as we on this side are, all the arguments about people not understanding the intricacies of pension funding versus non-funding, and all the complaints about a debate of this kind producing too many letters for some hon. members to deal with, do not set aside the fundamental fact that it is almost two years since a joint committee of both houses recommended action on behalf of retired civil servants, and nothing has been done. This is to the discredit of parliament and of the government for not providing an opportunity for dealing with this important measure.
I fully understand how the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) feels about this matter for he was the Commons chairman of the joint committee. He did a good job and all of us who were on that committee feel that faith was not kept. We feel that we had a right to believe that the recommendations we made would be acted upon, and for the government, now nearly two years later, to be amending these various superannuation acts without providing the increases that were
7022	COMMONS DEBATES	March 24, 1969
Statute Law Amendment Act
recommended and in fact promised, is a crying shame.
So far as this bill is concerned, as has been said on several occasions, we believe there are a number of good things in it. I think particularly of provisions for widows who will have their pensions reinstated if a second marriage results in a divorce. I think of the provisions for children who stay in school or at university to have their pensions continued until age 25. I also think of certain adjustments that have been made between these plans and the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan. All these things are good, and that is why we are prepared to vote for this legislation.
I still regret that by virtue of a vote taken earlier this afternoon the bill contains clauses which provide for the government to pay a higher rate of interest on the money in the funds but on the strict understanding that none of that additional money is to be used to pay higher pensions to those who are now retired. I think that is a trick that is unworthy of the government. However, even with that in it the bill has other measures that are good, and therefore we feel it should receive the support of the house. But I plead as earnestly as I can that the next time the government brings in a bill to amend these various superannuation acts it deal with the matters that we have been talking about.
I give the government three things to do. First, I propose that the government provide for an increase in the pensions of those who are now retired. Second, I propose that it build into the act an automatic clause that will escalate after retirement-and here I am referring to those who are now working-the pensions of retired civil servants and I propose that that escalation be in line with increases in wages and salaries. Third, I propose that the government change the rate of the widow's pension. Leaving it at only 50 per cent of the late husband's pension is quite unfair, particularly when in our own Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act the rate for a widow's pension is 60 per cent. As a matter of fact, I think the rate for widows of civil servants should be higher than that; I would say 75 per cent.
I hope there will be another bill amending the Public Service Superannuation Act soon- I hope it wiR come this session. Let it do the three things I mentioned: raise the pensions of those now retired, build in an automatic escalation clause, and increase the rate of pensions paid to widows.

speechtext:
That Bill C-172, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act, be amended by deleting from clause 7 at line 4, page 5, the words "five thousand" and substituting therefor the words "one thousand".
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the present time section 23 of the Financial Administration Act reads as follows, and I think I should put the whole section on record:
23 (1) The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, may, if he considers it in the public interest, delete from the accounts, in whole or in part, any obligation or debt due to Her Majesty or any claim by Her Majesty that does not exceed one thousand dollars.
(la) The Treasury Board may make regulations authorizing the deletion from the accounts of any obligation or debt due to Her Majesty or any claim by Her Majesty that does not exceed one hundred dollars.
(2) The obligations, debts and claims deleted from the public accounts under this section during any year shall be reported in the public accounts for that year.
March 24, 1969

The proposed amendment in Bill C-172 raises the regulatory right of the Treasury Board up to $5,000. It is my impression that at the present time-the minister may correct me if I am wrong-anything over $1,000 must be handled in a different way. In which way I am not sure at the moment except that it must be covered by an item in the estimates, particularly if it deals with taxes for which an assessment has been made or with a customs entry which has been made and has been incorporated into the revenue and there are figures on one side of the consolidated revenue accounts ledger which must be taken care of if it is then written off.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
My hon. friend from Wellington has proposed that notwithstanding the effects of inflation, and some so-called desire for administrative convenience, the ceiling remains at $1,000. The government wants to make it $5,000, and that is the difference between us.
Nothing is said about claims which do not exceed $100. The bill is lumping the two classes together, and frankly I do not see the purpose of doing so. Publication will, of course, continue to be made in the public accounts but I suggest parliament should have still greater control. I do not like this idea that the Treasury Board itself should have power to act. This is why we are proposing the amendment. If hon. members would like to refer to the evidence given before the committee I would draw their attention to the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence Nos. 10 and 11 and 12 where they may find a record of the discussion which took place. Having said this, I move that the amendment be accepted by the house. It does not involve a question of principle; it is a question of the amount. We would like to maintain the status quo as to the ceiling of the amount that can be written off under the act.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might say a word about this amendment. The current language of the act, which is set forth on page 9 of the bill, does not, unfortunately, provide for payments contracted for prior to the end of the fiscal year in respect of which there may have been no work performed, goods received or services rendered. The case cited before the committee was that of an author commissioned to write a book or an artist commissioned to paint or reproduce a work of art. It is the practice of the trade, if I may call it so, for a payment to be made on the signing of such a contract even though no work may have been done or no service rendered.
In order to cover this kind of eventuality it was proposed to amend the section so that it would read "for the purpose of discharging a debt that became due prior to the end of the fiscal year". In committee there was some opinion that the relationship of the debt to services should be made a little more explicit, as a consequence of which the amendment now proposed by my hon. friend was introduced. It has the effect of elaborating on the words "a debt that became due".
The section now refers to a debt "payable for work performed, goods received or services rendered prior to the end of the fiscal year", to which the following words are now added: "or payable under any other contractual arrangement prior to the end of that year". This covers the additional circumstances I have mentioned, to reflect current methods of doing business. I commend the amendment to the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Darlmouih-Halifax Easi) moved:
subtopic: MINAS BASIN-SUGGESTED EXPEDITING OF STUDY AND DECISION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of taking immediate steps in consultation with the proper provincial authorities to bring to a conclusion within the next twelve months, the feasibility study of Minas Basin tidal power and on the basis of the study make a decision to proceed, or otherwise, within six months of receiving the study.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my remarks on this subject could be very extensive or they could be brief. I intend to make them brief and to content myself with some four or five observations in connection with the study which is currently going on. I intend to relate my remarks to the development of the study which has taken place since the placing of this notice of motion on the order paper some six months ago, but before doing so I express the hope that the decision to provide more money for the study is a good omen for the province, bearing in mind the economic advantage which would flow from the development referred to in the motion.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The background to this on-going study which will culminate in June with a report to the government can very briefly be summed up in this way. In August, 1966, the federal authority and the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick agreed to launch what became known as feasibility studies by the Atlantic tidal power programming board. The programming board was made responsible for studying not only the physical but also the economic potential of the development of electric power from the massive tides in the Bay of Fundy and adjoining areas. Implicit also in the terms of reference of the committee was the very difficult and continuing task of studying and determining whether or not it would be feasible, assuming from an engineering point of view that it was, to transmit massive amounts of power to a ready and willing market.
These studies and their economic and physical or mechanical aspects have preoccupied the committee for some three years now. Indeed, so intensive did its work become that last year the board had to come back to its joint authority and seek additional
March 24, 1969

funds. At that time about $1 million was requested, and it is in the fact it was granted that I find the first glimmer of hope. There was no hesitation whatever on the part of the federal government or the provinces willingly to underwrite the additional amount of money required to complete the studies.
When these studies are completed-I think this must be understood by hon. members-it will be recommended to the three governments concerned that detailed studies should either be made or not made with a view to proceeding or not proceeding with such development. Indeed, in the terms of reference set down for the board was a very explicit and clear direction that the board should in its report include not only the details but the cost of additional studies. I assume those studies would relate to preliminary engineering work-ups, information about where the massive amounts of money required to finance this development could be found and at what cost. Perhaps because I am an optimist and believe that the report will be a positive one in all aspects, with the possible exception of that part of the report that deals with the cost of the money required, I hope that the three governments involved, but principally the senior government in Ottawa, will not in any way hesitate to extend these studies so that the question may be gone into in more depth, if only to determine at what stage this development could be proceeded with.
As I say, I believe the report will be a positive one. I do not think anybody questions the massive amount of electrical energy potentially contained in the tides of the Minas Basin, the Annapolis Basin and St. Mary's Basin, which were also included in these studies, as was Chignecto Bay. I think the report will indicate that it is possible from an engineering point of view to proceed, that the tidal regime itself is compatible with harnessing, that sedimentation-control over deposits on the floor of these basins

will not pose any real problem, that the massive amount of potential energy in the tides can be harnessed and transmitted economically, that there will be no detrimental effect on the fisheries or on transportation, for example, in these three specific areas and that the chief concern will be with regard to the cost of the capital required. If the report that is brought down is favourable in the directions I have indicated, I hope the government will not hesitate to authorize on-going studies to determine where the money required can be borrowed, at what cost, and to what extent the federal authority

The benefits of this development to the Atlantic provinces are sufficient to excite the hearts and souls of anyone who has had to live, work and struggle industrially in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. At last year's federal-provincial constitutional conference the premier of Nova Scotia, the Hon. G. I. Smith, among other points made a very real and continuing one. It was he who sounded the call to arms, so to speak, for all Canadians to act in the national sense in order to reduce the incidence and magnitude of regional disparity. Indeed, so clear was the premier's plea in this regard that the government responded positively. I am not giving all the credit to our premier but it was he who first spoke out publicly and most forcefully. As I say, the government responded in a positive sense, and as a result the house is now considering the proposal to establish a regional desk, the department of regional affairs.
One premise to which the premier is dedicated is implicit in his urgent call, and I suppose it is a key segment of any plan to reorganize our economy with federal help. It is that Canada is only as strong as its provinces. You cannot have national unity as long as you have disparity of the magnitude that exists in Canada today. It exists most notably, of course, in the rural parts of Quebec and in the Atlantic provinces. One way, indeed the only real way, to overcome it within a reasonable period of time and without massive subsidies for programs fulfilling varied requirements would be by reacting positively to the report of the tidal programming board and for the government to become involved in the capital expenditures required for the building of dams and hydroelectric generating systems.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
If the cost of money will make the carrying out of this program prohibitive I suggest we could subsidize the cost. There is nothing inconsistent about that. If that is not done the people of Canada for a long time will pour money on a massive scale into various programs for the Atlantic region until, accidentally, one is found that works. That is not good enough. The hydroelectric power potential of the Minas Basin and the Bay of Fundy in general is unmatched. If we could tap it the electrical power produced would exceed by an almost immeasurable margin all the electric power produced in Canada in 1969.

So fantastic and so encouraging are preliminary reports that that statement stands, I think, without contradiction. In practical terms it means that with such power available reduction industries which need massive amounts of power could be set up in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to employ our people, not in groups of five or ten but in thousands. That is what we require. We have hundreds of industries in the Atlantic provinces but each employs only a handful of people. We need large industries employing thousands of people so that we can build up our markets and so that the port of Halifax will have a viable reason to continue as a port. The port is on deep water, and a spinoff effect of these huge new industries would be the revitalization of one of our most viable industries at present, the port of Halifax.
I reiterate that it is necessary for the government to react favourably to the report which, to judge from what I know, will be a favourable one. I therefore suggest that the government ought to react positively by making clear at an early date that if the cost of money is the only serious impediment to carrying out the program it will consider subsidizing that cost and will involve itself in this development.
The final part of my notice of motion calls on the government to make a decision to proceed or otherwise with this project within six months of receiving the study. I have included that wording because the passage of time concerns us. We do not want to wait 15 or 20 years for someone to say that the money market is favourable and if the program is begun then it will be finished within seven or eight years. If the study is positive the project should not be shelved but proceeded with as soon as the government has had an opportunity to look into all its implications. I make this suggestion because I know it will take a certain amount of time before a final decision can be taken. In any event, I hope that by January 1, 1970, the government will be deeply involved in the on-going studies that will result if the terms of reference of the feasibility study have been met. I invite hon. members to support this notice of motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) for bringing this matter to the attention of the house during private members' hour. It is an important subject and has been debated at


least twice during the time I have been in the house. I was happy to speak on it on previous occasions.
As was pointed out, in August, 1966, the government of Canada entered into an agreement with the governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to study the feasibility of power development in the Minas Basin area and Shepody Basin. The present notice of motion asks the government to consider the advisability of taking immediate steps in consultation with the proper provincial authorities to bring to a conclusion within the next 12 months the feasibility study regarding tidal power development which has been mentioned previously and to make a decision on that project.
The agreement signed in August, 1966, indicated that the feasibility study probably would be finished by June 30. Perhaps it will not be possible for that to be done. Nevertheless, up to now it has been understood that the study will be completed by June 30. Once it has been completed the government of Canada, in conjunction with the provinces involved, will have to decide if the report is positive and favourable. The government of Canada will then have to decide how it will help the provinces to finance the project. Should the report be positive it will mean that the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia will have a great potential opportunity to sell power to the United States. It will also show how important the Bay of Fundy area is to the development of tidal power.
If the report is positive and favourable we should consider not only the development of electric power but also the opportunities for employment that will be opened up in the Atlantic region. Employment opportunities will be created in the building of these power installations as well as after they have been finished.
The government has committed itself to the idea of reducing regional disparities in this country. Before the present house there is a bill setting up the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The minister who will be in charge of this department has already said that economic expansion by itself does not mean much without the co-operation and co-ordination of all government programs. This fact has been brought before the house many times during the debate on the reorganization bill. It has also been brought to the attention of the Standing Committee on Regional Development. As mentioned by the
March 24, 1969	COMMONS
hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, the employment created by such a project would be as good and possibly better than subsidizing 10 or 15 industries in New Brunswick or Nova Scotia.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
This is an area where the government by its planning and co-ordination of programs can assist the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. The decision to finance this project and to assist the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia will have to take into account the good these projects can do to the economy. The rate for power will be reduced enormously and it will help our balance of payments. The government will have to be consistent because this is one way to help the economy of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. We had a example in New Brunswick in the last three or four years in the Mac-taquac power project which assisted the payroll of New Brunswick enormously. The fact that many people were employed on that project for three or four years will have to be taken into consideration.
I would like to say a few words with regard to the power aspect. The Bay of Fundy is one of the few places in the world where tides range up to 52 feet. The bay is about 50 miles wide at its mouth and is about 180 miles long ending in two arms, Minas Basin and Chignecto Bay. It is because of these enormous tides that the subject of power development was raised. The question has been raised as to how important tidal waves are in power development.
An enormous amount of energy is contained in the daily movement of tides throughout the world. Tidal power dissipated by friction and eddies alone has been estimated as being roughly comparable to all of the economically exploitable power potential of the rivers of the world. A power development project seems to be feasible in the Bay of Fundy.
I hope that in presenting this motion the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East was not suggesting that the study should be stopped within 12 months. The Atlantic Tidal Power Development Board may require more time than that. I think the hon. member's point is that the project should not be forgotten with the conclusion of the study. If the report is positive, I will support the building of this project as soon as possible. However, it would be subject to priorities. As I stated, the government will have to study it from an

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) for having again brought this matter to the attention of the house. The hon. member has implied that the study begun several years ago is progressing well. The motion asks that the study be brought to a conclusion within 12 months and a decision made on whether the project will be proceeded with.
I have always been impressed with the amount of power estimated to be contained in the tides of the Bay of Fundy. It has been the source of engineering inspiration for many years. I am surprised that the study has now reached a cost of $1 million without any indication to the people of this country of what is being achieved. If $1J million is to be spent on a study of this great natural resource, it is time for the people involved in the study to put forth some information as to their findings and the findings of other countries in this regard. I understand that considerable work has been done in this field in at least two other countries, in Holland where power was generated from a similar source and in Madagascar where a large experiment was sponsored by the French government. The French have also experimented in their own country.
I was interested to hear of the potential that this project has for this area. I disagree with the hon. member on the government side who suggested that this project should be proceeded with soon in order that the power may be sold elsewhere. This is a typical solution to power development in the normal sense. At Hamilton Falls, where there really is no industry, we talk about establishing and expanding our national grid by permitting the sale of that power. Surely that is not what we want in the maritimes. In the maritimes the development of this natural resource should provide a source of inspiration for the development of industry.
Unless the study reaches a decision with regard to developing secondary industry in that area, the quantity of power produced will only mean cheaper power for cities such as Toronto, Montreal, Boston and New York. It really will not assist in the development of the maritimes. I hope the study will take into consideration the aspiration of the people of

[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I believe it will be found that we are much too late in developing just another cheap power resource. I think of a number of statements that were made when the Saskatchewan River project was being developed. I sat in on a meeting when the former premier of that province had a discussion with his finance minister about the cost of developing power on the Saskatchewan River. He pointed out at that time that power could be developed from a thermal plant probably two mills cheaper than by the hydro plants on the Saskatchewan River. The decision to go ahead with the Saskatchewan River project did not hinge on the power development but on the total change in the economy of the whole area this project would bring about. That again raises the point of whether or not this project was 50 years too late. The irrigation part of the project was a dream of the people on the prairies in the dust bowl days because it would have perhaps alleviated the depression in that area which was probably worse than in any other part of Canada.
For many years the people of the maritimes have been working very hard to develop the economy of their area. I hope that this power development, if it takes place and when it takes place, will not be a power development for the sake of power but that it will be for the sake of the natural resource around which a totally new and vibrant economy could be created. If we are only to become involved in establishing grids, I feel quite strongly the people of the maritimes will get absolutely nothing out of the expenditure except the labour force that is involved in producing it. My area has probably the only .large power developments that are taking place in Ontario or which will take place in the future. We are putting that power into the major cities, thereby defeating the problem we are trying to solve which is to bring industry into the area. We are doing this because the project which is worth $40 million will employ 2,000 or 3,000 people on a temporary basis,. When the plant is in operation it will employ 30 or 40 people. It will be a cheap source of electricity for the industrial area of Ontario and the United States.
I hope the house will agree to accept the motion of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), and in doing so will be cognizant of the particular value this


development could have in relation to the total economy of the maritime provinces. I strongly urge hon. members who are interested to remember that if the only purpose of the project is the production of cheap power, that probably could be produced in a much better way in other areas. If the purpose of the federal government and provincial governments, in co-operation with the minister of regional development, is the development of a secondary industry which would rely on the hydro-electric resource being developed by this project, then the project will be worthy of the support of every member in this house. If it is to be only a cheap source of power for export purposes, I for one think we should only consider the engineering feasibility of the project and not the practicality of developing electricity. If this project will produce a resource which will be able to solve many of the problems of the maritimes, it will be of benefit to this area. However, if it is only for the purpose of providing cheap electric power, it will provide very little revenue for that area.
At the same time the power produced will be of value to the areas which will be in competition with this area.

I would like to quote from an editorial by Michael Wardell, in the Atlantic Advocate, on this subject. He has been secretary of the Chignecto Canal Committee and has studied this project from its very beginning. He wrote:
The tidal power of Chignecto Bay is likely to be for all time the cheapest power, inexhaustible, and once established becoming ever cheaper in terms of real values that rise in relation to money.
It should be used for providing the peaks of power integrated by means of a grid with Arm power supplied from thermal, hydro or atomic generators.
While I do not wish to take anything away from the importance of the Minas Basin tidal project, and while I do support the hon. member in his appeal for a study, I would point out that it is a much larger undertaking than the one nearby that has been studied in great detail.
Writing in an editorial in the Atlantic Advocate of December, 1964, Brigadier Wardell said as follows:
Alongside is Minas Basin, another tidal project so huge that it daunts the hearts of our planners even to think of it. It has the attractive by-product of a road which might be laid across the dam to connect the area of Cumberland county to the Annapolis valley.
It is known that it is feasible to produce electric power by harnessing these tremendous tides of the Bay of Fundy. A joint United States-Canada study was made of the Quoddy project near the border of Maine and New Brunswick on the same Bay of Fundy. In the report of the International Joint Commission dated April, 1961, a similar project there was declared to be fully feasible.
There is no doubt that the impact of the development of one of these projects on the economy of the Maritime provinces would be immense. Much additional employment would be created during the period of construction. But it is the permanent prosperity following the completion of the plan that would raise the standards of the region for all time. There is a general belief that it would contribute tremendously to the development of the Maritime provinces.
The provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have vast wealth in natural resources. Nova Scotia has rich deposits of gypsum and coal in great quantity. It also has more than 10 million acres of forest land and New Brunswick has over 15 million acres of forest land and 17 billion cubic feet of merchantable timber. A recent report of the government of New Brunswick stated that annual
